name: Dana Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say is confidential. Could you start with a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the customer team at FreshCart, an online grocery delivery firm, in their contact centre on the business park behind the big roundabout. It's missing eggs, squashed bread, a driver who turned up two hours late, and arguments about whether oat milk is a fair swap for semi-skimmed. Half chats, half calls.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being quick. I use the AI reply tool every shift and I've set up my own shortcuts in it, so I clear more chats than most of the floor. What wears me out is the night shifts before holidays, when everyone's turkey is missing at once.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm married to Imran, he's a pharmacy technician at the hospital. On weekends I help my mum with her catering, samosas and biryani trays for weddings and mosque dinners, and I've started taking the bookings online. We've got about four months saved, and we pray it stays that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it stays a clever helper, like my reply tool. That's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool and people should stop being scared of it. At the mosque some of the aunties think AI is something sinister, and I'd tell them it's mostly autocomplete. Online I'd post a few tips, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it suits me. I'm already faster because of it, and FreshCart's growing because people are lazy about shopping. My job looks fine, and the weekend catering is the bit I really care about growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tool and try for a team leader spot. I'd use AI on the catering side too, writing menus and replying to wedding enquiries at night. I'd want to get Mum's bookings from two weddings a month to four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the catering earn right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three hundred a month for me after ingredients, more in wedding season. It's not much, but it's ours. My mum has been cooking for forty years and only now has a website.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people are lazy about shopping. Is that a criticism?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. My mum walks to the market every Saturday and haggles. But laziness pays my wages, so I won't complain too loudly.

I'd tell the mosque aunties it's mostly **autocomplete**.
think: My **job looks fine**, and FreshCart is growing.
The weekend **catering** is the part I really want to grow.

Use AI to answer **wedding enquiries** for Mum's catering.
Grow catering bookings from **two to four** weddings a month.

steps.text: Apply for team leader on the FreshCart customer team
Grow Mum's catering to four weddings a month
Use AI to write menus and answer wedding enquiries at night

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers. Well, FreshCart's already halfway there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms have every right to run leaner, that's business. But I'd also say the people let go should be helped to start something, not just handed a form. I'd post about how I'm using AI for Mum's catering, to show it can work for small people too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think FreshCart would cut the floor by two-thirds within a few years. My numbers are good, but the AI tool I'm good at is the tool that replaces us on the FreshCart floor. If they offered voluntary redundancy, I'd honestly take it and put the money into the catering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask HR quietly what a redundancy payout would look like for five years' service. I'd keep saving, aiming for six months, so the business has a cushion. I'd start registering the catering properly, food hygiene certificate, insurance, the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little nervous, but more excited than scared. It feels like a push I've needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family say about you leaving a steady job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Imran would worry, he likes things steady. My dad would say a job with a pension is a gift from God. But my mum would be on my side, because she's been waiting for someone to take the business on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at FreshCart?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Agnes, who's sixty and does the phone line for older customers. She doesn't type fast. I'd want her to stay on that line, because the older customers trust her voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. That's very fast. Faster than a lot of people can handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for ordinary families, and I'd say it plainly. But I wouldn't say ban it, because whoever bans it just falls behind. At the mosque I'd say we need to help each other find work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my FreshCart job's gone, probably within a year of it arriving. The catering is hands-on, cooking and serving, so it lasts until about 2031 when the robots come. The scary part is whether people still have money for big weddings if half of them lose their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave FreshCart before I'm pushed and go full time on the catering with Mum. I'd spend about two thousand of our savings on a second-hand commercial oven and a hire kitchen two days a week. I'd let AI run the bookings, the invoices and the social media so I only cook and serve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. Not panicked, because I'd have a plan. But tense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Imran the night you decided?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my husband Imran his hospital wage keeps us safe for now, and I'll make the catering pay within a year. He'd ask what happens if it doesn't. I'd say then I'll work in someone else's kitchen, because people will still eat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI first, robots three years later. How does that change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office half of my life goes straight away and the cooking half gets three more years. So I'd use the AI to run the office half of the catering for free. After 2031, I don't know, I'd have to see what a robot can do with a samosa.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** for ordinary families.
I wouldn't say **ban it**, because whoever bans it falls behind.
think: My **FreshCart job** is gone within a year of AGI arriving.
Fewer people may afford **big weddings** if half of them lose jobs.
do: Leave FreshCart **before being pushed** and cater full time with Mum.
Spend about **two thousand** on an oven and a hire kitchen.
Let AI handle **bookings and invoices** so I just cook.
feel: **Tense** but not panicked, because she has a **plan**.
S2.quote: The office half of my life goes straight away and the cooking half gets three more years.
fieldNote: She expects to lose the **contact centre job** but has already planned her exit.
Her worry moves to **customers' incomes**: weddings shrink when guests lose work.
She'd use AI to **automate** her own small business while cooking stays hands-on.

steps.text: Hand in notice at FreshCart and cater full time with Mum
Buy a used commercial oven and rent a kitchen two days a week
Set up AI to handle catering bookings, invoices and social media

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a proper runway. I like that one better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for anyone willing to work to land somewhere. I'd tell younger cousins to learn a skill with their hands and use AI for the paperwork. Firms and families should plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it's close to perfect for me. Two years at FreshCart saving and learning, then the catering full time. By 2031 I'd want a small unit with my name on the door, and the robots not due till about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at FreshCart for two years and put most of my wage into savings and kit. I'd take on a second cook, my cousin Sana, on weekends. I'd use AI to price every menu so we stop under-charging, which Mum always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful and a bit impatient. I'd want to start yesterday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Other people's jobs, really. If everyone in the area loses office work, fewer people book caterers for a nephew's birthday. A business is only as good as its customers' wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your mum under-charges. How would she take AI pricing her food?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd hate it at first. She charges what feels fair to the families she knows. I'd show her the numbers and she'd say fine, but not for the mosque dinners, those stay cheap.

I'd tell younger cousins to learn a **hands-on skill**.

I'd want a **small unit** with my name on it by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's comfortable. 2036 and robots in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse not to prepare. People who wait for the government to fix it will be disappointed. Get a skill, start something, help your family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the version I'd sleep best in. I could build the catering slowly and keep FreshCart's wage until it goes. Imran and I would probably have our first child in that time too, so slow is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at FreshCart for three or four years and grow the catering in the evenings and weekends. We'd buy a house with a big kitchen, which helps both the business and the family. I'd keep using AI for everything I can, because the people who start early stay ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Properly calm. Like we'd have room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when the robots come for kitchen work around 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By the time robots come for kitchen work, I'd want to be the owner, not the cook. Maybe I'd buy a robot myself. My mum would never let one near her biryani, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a child change your plans for the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would slow them a little. But Mum looked after me in the kitchen while she cooked, and I'd do the same. That's how my family has always worked.

Slow change fits having our **first child** in that time.

Buy a house with a **big kitchen** for business and family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, not for my job, which I'd leave anyway, but for my customers. If half the town loses office jobs at once, nobody books a caterer. What would help is cheap small-business loans and fewer rules for home kitchens, so people can start things quickly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether faith and family help. They do, a lot. When someone at our mosque lost their job last year, five families sent food for a month, and nobody needed a form for that.

headlineQuote: When someone at our mosque lost their job last year, five families sent food for a month, and nobody needed a form for that.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old** customer service agent at FreshCart, an online grocery delivery firm.
She uses AI **every day** and is among the fastest on the floor.
She's married to Imran, a hospital **pharmacy technician**, and helps her mother run a small **catering** business.
In every AI picture she plans to **leave first** and grow the catering, using AI for the office side.
Her main worry is her **customers' wages**, not her own job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because if half the town loses office jobs, nobody books a caterer.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **small-business loans** and fewer rules for **home kitchens**.
